title: Bits as a table, and reversing them
sub: Counting Bits as a first taste of dynamic programming, Reverse Bits, the sign-copying shift and the >>> that Unity lacks
cards/0/title: Counting Bits: the problem and the brute-force loop
cards/0/body:
Counting Bits (LeetCode #338): for every i from 0 to n, return the number of 1s in i; n ≤ 10⁵. The answer is an array of n + 1 numbers. The extra requirement: O(n) and no built-in popcount.

Brute force counts the 1s of every i with the Kernighan loop from the first lesson. Each number takes as many steps as it has 1s — on average half its length. In total that is O(n log n), about 10⁶ steps for n = 10⁵. That is fast, but the interviewer wants O(n): one operation per number.

The signal: the answer for i can be built from the answer for a smaller number that is already computed. That is dynamic programming: a state (bits[i]), a transition (how bits[i] is expressed through smaller ones), an order (from smaller to larger) and a base (bits[0] = 0). DP is covered in depth in the “Backtracking and dynamic programming” unit; this is its simplest case.
cards/1/q: How many inner-loop steps in total does this solution take for n = 2¹⁶ − 1 = 65,535?
cards/1/options/0: 524,288 = 16 · 2¹⁵: each bit is set in exactly half of the numbers
cards/1/explain: The numbers 0 to 2¹⁶ − 1 are all the 16-bit numbers, and each of the 16 bits is set in exactly half of them: 16 · 32,768 = 524,288 steps, 8 per number on average — half the length. That is O(n log n): fast, but not O(n).
cards/1/wrong/1: One step per number would mean a single 1 in every number. Kernighan takes a step per 1 bit.
cards/1/wrong/2: 16 steps per number is a loop over every bit. Kernighan skips the zeros: 8 on average.
cards/2/title: The key idea: drop the last bit
cards/2/body:
i >> 1 is i without its last bit: 13 = 1101₂ → 110₂ = 6. It has the same 1s as i, except for the last bit. So bits[i] = bits[i >> 1] + (i & 1). For i ≥ 1, i >> 1 < i always holds, so going up in order we always take an answer that is already there.

Invariant: before step i, all of bits[0..i−1] in the table are correct. One operation per number — O(n) time, and the only memory is the answer itself.

A second transition uses Kernighan: i & (i − 1) is smaller than i and has one 1 less, so bits[i] = bits[i & (i − 1)] + 1. Also O(n). The shape of the table shows too: a power of two 2ᵏ has a single 1, and the numbers 2ᵏ..2ᵏ⁺¹ − 1 repeat 0..2ᵏ − 1 with one extra 1.
cards/3/explain: The answer covers 0 to n inclusive, n + 1 slots; new already gives bits[0] = 0. i >> 1 is smaller than i and already computed, and (i & 1) adds back the dropped last bit. bits[i − 1] + 1 is wrong: 7 → 8 clears three 1s and sets one. i << 1 is larger than i — it is not in the table yet.
cards/4/task: Step through the trace on n = 12: the table fills from left to right, and each number takes its answer from i >> 1. The rig asks twice what goes into the table.
cards/4/goal/asks/0/q: The table up to 7 is done, bits[7] = 3. What goes into bits[8]?
cards/4/goal/asks/0/explain: 8 = 1000₂, 8 >> 1 = 4 = 100₂, and the last bit is 0. bits[8] = bits[4] + 0 = 1 — a power of two has a single 1. “The previous one plus one” is not always right: 7 → 8 clears three 1s with the carry and sets one.
cards/4/goal/asks/1/explain: 11 >> 1 = 5 = 101₂ has two 1s, and the last bit of 11 that got dropped is a 1. bits[11] = bits[5] + 1 = 3: 1011₂ has three 1s.
cards/5/body:
Reverse Bits (#190): reverse the 32 bits of a number — bit 0 becomes bit 31, bit 1 becomes bit 30, and so on. 1 → 0x80000000 = 2,147,483,648. Work with a uint; if the number comes in as an int, cast it. LeetCode currently uses the signature int ReverseBits(int n) with n even and 0 ≤ n ≤ 2³¹ − 2: bit 0 is zero, so the answer fits in an int. Still reverse a uint inside: return (int)ReverseBits((uint)n);, calling the uint overload below.

The loop: take the lowest bit of n (n & 1), shift it into the result from the right (r = (r << 1) | bit), and shift n right. Over the next 31 shifts the first bit taken travels up to bit 31. There are exactly 32 steps, even if n runs out of 1s earlier: the leading zeros of n are the trailing zeros of the result, and without them the answer ends up not shifted far enough.
cards/6/q: This reversal returns 1 for n = 1, but it should return 2,147,483,648. Tap the line with the bug.
cards/6/explain: The loop stops as soon as n has no 1s left — for n = 1, right after the first step. But that 1 still has to travel 31 positions left: the leading zeros of n are the trailing zeros of the answer. It must be exactly 32 steps: for (int i = 0; i < 32; i++).
cards/7/title: Shifts in C#: sign, >>> and width
cards/7/body:
The sign-copying shift. >> on int and long is arithmetic: a copy of the sign bit comes in from the left, −8 >> 1 = −4, and −1 >> k = −1 for any k. On uint and ulong it is logical: zeros come in. When you want “just bits”, use an unsigned type.

>>>, the unsigned shift for signed types, only arrived in C# 11 (.NET 7). Unity is on C# 9 and does not have it: write (int)((uint)x >> k).

Shift width. For an int only the 5 low bits of the count are used: 1 << 32 == 1, 1 << 40 == 256; for a long, 6 bits. The shift happens in the type of the left operand, so 64 bits need 1L << k or 1UL << k. And long f = 1 << 31 is −2³¹: the int came out negative, and widening it to long copied the sign into bits 32–63.
cards/7/code:
int x = -8;
int a = x >> 1;                  // -4: the sign was copied
int b = (int)((uint)x >> 1);     // 2147483644: C# 9, same as x >>> 1 in C# 11
int s = 40;
int c = 1 << s;                  // 256: an int takes the count modulo 32
long d = 1 << s;                 // 256: shifted as an int, widened afterwards
long e = 1L << s;                // 1099511627776
long f = 1 << 31;                // -2147483648 = 0xFFFFFFFF80000000
cards/8/q: You need a mask of the k lowest 1s, k from 0 to 32: int mask = (1 << k) - 1. Where does this code go wrong?
cards/8/options/0: At k = 32: the mask is 0 instead of −1 (all ones), because 1 << 32 == 1
cards/8/options/1: At k = 31: overflow and an OverflowException
cards/8/options/2: Nowhere: the mask is right for every k from 0 to 32
cards/8/explain: An int takes the shift count modulo 32: 1 << 32 is 1 << 0 = 1, and the mask becomes 1 − 1 = 0. You need a special case, k == 32 ? -1 : (1 << k) - 1, or a shift in long: (int)((1L << k) - 1).
cards/8/wrong/1: 1 << 31 = int.MinValue, and minus 1 wraps to int.MaxValue, which is 31 ones — exactly what you want. No exception: subtraction is unchecked by default.
cards/8/wrong/2: At k = 32 the shift moves nothing: a count of 32 modulo 32 is 0.
cards/9/body:
The loop takes 32 iterations. Faster is swapping blocks: the 16-bit halves, the bytes within them, then nibbles, pairs and neighbouring bits. 5 steps = log₂ 32, each with two shifts and an OR, plus two ANDs from the second step on; no loop and no branches. The mask picks the lower block of each pair: 0x00FF00FF is the low byte of each half, 0x0F0F0F0F the low nibble of each byte, 0x33333333 = 0011…₂, 0x55555555 = 0101…₂.

If the function is called many times (the problem’s follow-up), use a 256-entry table of reversed bytes: four lookups and a merge. Unity.Mathematics has a ready-made math.reversebits. .NET has no portable bit reversal (only the ARM intrinsic ArmBase.ReverseElementBits), and BinaryPrimitives.ReverseEndianness reverses the bytes, not the bits — do not mix them up.
cards/9/deep:
Why this is a reversal. A bit’s position is a 5-bit number b₄b₃b₂b₁b₀. Swapping halves flips b₄, swapping bytes flips b₃, and so on. After five steps all five digits of the position are flipped: bit i has moved to 31 − i. The same “spread the bits with masks” trick builds a Morton code — interleaving the bits of x and y (x = (x | (x << 8)) & 0x00FF00FF, then 4, 2, 1 with the masks 0x0F0F0F0F, 0x33333333, 0x55555555). A Morton code orders grid cells along a Z-curve: neighbouring cells tend to sit close together in memory, which is why it is used as a key in spatial hashes and quadtrees, and GPUs use similar layouts for textures.

Where bit reversal shows up in games. The bit-reversed index permutation is the first step of an FFT (an audio spectrum for a visualiser, procedural noise); a bit-reversed counter gives the van der Corput sequence — evenly spread points for sampling without randomness.

Cost. The loop is 32 iterations, each depending on the previous one; swapping blocks is 5 steps, 23 operations; the table is 4 memory accesses. In an interview the loop plus a mention of block swapping is enough. Rotation, a related operation, is BitOperations.RotateLeft in .NET Core 3.0+ and math.rol in Unity.
cards/10/q: You are solving Counting Bits out loud. Put the steps in order.
cards/10/items/0: Clarify: n up to 10⁵, the answer is an array of n + 1 numbers, no built-in popcount
cards/10/items/1: Brute force: Kernighan for every i — O(n log n)
cards/10/items/2: Idea: i >> 1 is smaller than i and already computed — bits[i] = bits[i >> 1] + (i & 1)
cards/10/items/3: Code: an array of n + 1, a loop from 1, base bits[0] = 0
cards/10/items/4: Run it: bits[5] = bits[2] + 1 = 2, bits[6] = bits[3] + 0 = 2
cards/10/items/5: Complexity: O(n) time, the only memory is the answer
cards/10/items/6: Edge cases: n = 0 → [0]; the second transition is bits[i & (i − 1)] + 1
cards/10/explain: State, transition, order and base are the whole story of a DP: name them explicitly. The second transition at the end shows you understand the idea rather than remember one formula.
cards/11/q: Match the task to the expression.
cards/11/pairs/4/0: Reverse the bytes, not the bits
